clinical_knowledge.topic: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (classic triad of 'wet, wobbly, and wacky'), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive walking instability, urinary urgency, and forgetfulness over 6 months

Key HPI features: 72M presents with a 6-month history of progressive walking difficulty described as 'sticky feet' (gait apraxia), frequent urinary urgency and occasional wetting, and mild short-term memory forgetfulness.

Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (classic triad of 'wet, wobbly, and wacky').
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Parkinson's disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: rapid progression, headache, or focal deficits, which are atypical for NPH and require urgent imaging to exclude an alternate diagnosis.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (classic triad of 'wet, wobbly, and wacky')
Obtain brain MRI to assess for ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy and exclude alternative structural causes before CSF testing.
If appropriate after imaging and specialist assessment, perform a large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) with pre- and post-tap gait assessment.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 72-year-old man with 6 months of progressive walking instability described as 'sticky feet' (gait apraxia), urinary urgency with occasional incontinence, and mild short-term memory forgetfulness.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (classic triad of 'wet, wobbly, and wacky').
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (classic triad of 'wet, wobbly, and wacky').
reference_soap.plan: Obtain brain MRI to assess for ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy and exclude alternative structural causes. If appropriate after imaging and specialist assessment, perform a large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) with pre- and post-tap gait assessment. Refer to neurosurgery or neurology for consideration of shunting if testing supports NPH, and provide patient counseling.

teaching.one_liner: The classic 'wet, wobbly, and wacky' triad of urinary urgency, gait apraxia, and mild cognitive decline, potentially reversible with a shunt.
red_flags: Rapidly progressive symptoms, which are atypical for NPH and suggest an alternate diagnosis
Focal neurological deficits not explained by the classic triad

must_ask.say: How would you describe your walking difficulty—for example, do your feet feel stuck to the floor?
How many months has this progressed?
What worries you about losing independence?

history.answer: Doctor, over the past six months I've become very unsteady on my feet, and I've been feeling forgetful and having trouble getting to the bathroom in time.
My wife is waiting right outside in the hall. She noticed my walking troubles before I did, so please feel free to talk to her.
It started about six months ago and has been gradually getting worse. It didn't happen overnight or in sudden steps; it just creeps up week after week.
My legs feel heavy, like my feet are glued to the floor when I try to start walking. I shuffle with small steps and feel off-balance, especially when turning.
I haven't had a hard fall yet, but I've tripped a couple of times over the living room carpet and had to catch myself on the furniture.
I misplace my keys or glasses and forget what my wife asked me to buy at the store ten minutes earlier. I can remember my childhood and old friends just fine, though.
I still know where I am and I don't get lost around the neighborhood. Sometimes it takes me an extra moment to find a word or calculate a bill, but I can manage.
I stopped driving three months ago because my feet felt too slow to hit the brake safely. I can dress and bathe myself, but everything takes me twice as long.
When I feel the urge to pee, I have to hurry right away or I can't hold it. I've had a few embarrassing accidents over the last two months where I couldn't reach the toilet in time.
My bowel movements are regular and normal. I have not had any bowel incontinence or constipation.
No, my alertness stays steady throughout the day. I don't have sudden confused episodes or days where I'm completely lost.
I haven't had any anger outbursts or paranoia, and I definitely don't see things that aren't there. My wife says I'm just a little quieter and slower than usual.
I wouldn't say I'm depressed, just frustrated that my body isn't cooperating. I still enjoy reading the newspaper and watching baseball.
My appetite is good, and I sleep well at night, though I do have to get up once or twice to use the bathroom.
No, I haven't bumped my head or had any head injuries. I don't have headaches either.
No, neither side feels weak or numb. My arms and hands work normally, and my speech isn't slurred at all.
My hands don't shake when they are resting on my lap, and I don't feel stiff like a robot. It's just my feet having trouble lifting off the floor.
No, I'm not sensitive to the cold, my skin hasn't been dry, and my weight has been completely stable.
No fever, chills, cough, or burning pain when I pass urine.
I haven't left the stove on or wandered off, but I worry about falling down when my feet feel stuck.
I was wondering if I might be developing Parkinson's disease or Alzheimer's, because my walking and memory are both getting worse.
I'm really terrified of losing my independence and becoming a burden on my wife if this keeps progressing.
I hope we can get a brain scan to find out what's causing this and see if there is any treatment that can help.
I've had high blood pressure for about ten years, but it's well controlled. No history of diabetes, stroke, or heart attacks.
I had my appendix removed when I was in college, and no other surgeries or hospital stays since.
I take amlodipine 5 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure. I don't take any sleeping pills, pain relievers, or over-the-counter supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I might have half a glass of wine on special family occasions, but essentially I don't drink alcohol.
I am a retired accountant, and I live comfortably at home in a single-story house with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure, and my mother passed away in her late eighties. Neither of them had dementia or Parkinson's disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Elderly gentleman sitting comfortably, alert and cooperative, with mildly slow body movements and no acute distress.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; MMSE score 25/30 with points lost on delayed recall and serial subtractions, with mild psychomotor slowing.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact, pupils equal and reactive, normal extraocular movements, and fundoscopy reveals no papilledema.
Normal muscle bulk and tone in all four extremities, motor strength 5/5 throughout, with no cogwheel rigidity or spasticity.
No resting tremor, postural tremor, or action tremor observed.
Intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in both upper and lower extremities; Romberg test is negative.
Deep tendon reflexes 2+ and symmetric bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally without Babinski sign.
Wide-based, short-stepped shuffling gait with magnetic quality, hesitancy initiating steps, and multi-step turning; finger-to-nose coordination is preserved.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and smooth without palpable masses, nodules, or tenderness.
